title: Indra and deep sleep
hookLine: Indra's third try: dreamless sleep, and the bliss that wants nothing
carry: ananda: the peace that wants nothing

cards: Thirty-two more years with Prajapati. Then a third answer. When someone is fast asleep, whole and at peace, and sees no dream: that is the self.
No pain there, no chasing, no tears. He started home. And for the third time, he stopped on the road.
In deep sleep, he thought, nobody knows anything. Not 'this is me.' Not the beings around. It's as if the self has simply gone out.

teach.b: Here the Mandukya gives an answer Indra didn't have on the road. Its fifth verse: where the sleeper desires no desire and sees no dream, that is deep sleep. And deep sleep isn't nothing.
Its self is called prajna, the knowing one. It has become one, a single mass of knowing, made of bliss, enjoying bliss. Why a mass of knowing?

teach.h: THE SOURCE OF WAKING AND DREAM.
teach.b: In waking you know a world; in dream you know images. In deep sleep there's nothing to know, so the knowing isn't spread among things. It's gathered, like light with nothing to fall on.
Commentators say that's why people wake up and say, I slept so well. Something was there to enjoy it. Verse six goes further: this quarter is the source and the end of beings.
Shankara explains that waking and dream come out of it every morning and fold back into it every night. In om, it's m, the lips closing. So Indra was half right.
Deep sleep isn't the final self, and he kept going, and so does the Mandukya.

teach.h: ANANDA: PEACE WITH NOTHING IN IT.
teach.b: But it shows what Hindus call ananda, bliss: the deepest peace comes with no objects at all. No wanting. An older Upanishad says that in deep sleep a father is no longer a father, a thief no longer a thief.
Today, rest gets sold as a product: the right app, the right pillow, one more purchase. The Mandukya points at what happens every night for free. When wanting stops, peace is already there.
Many Vedanta teachers put it simply: that peace isn't made by things. It's what you are underneath them.

how: Some Vedanta teachers use the everyday report 'I slept well' as a starting point for reflecting on deep sleep as the Mandukya's third quarter, prajna.

o: a medical text on sleep and the body's rest
a guide to the rites performed at nightfall
an Upanishad calling deep sleep a mass of knowing

s: Indra took deep sleep as the final answer
he worried the self had simply gone out, and turned back a third time.
the Mandukya says deep sleep is simply nothing
it calls it a single mass of knowing, made of bliss.
in deep sleep the sleeper desires nothing and sees no dream
verse five: that is deep sleep, the field of prajna.

games.q: you wake up and say 'I slept so well.' but you weren't aware of anything. how does the Mandukya explain it?
o: deep sleep is a mass of knowing, made of bliss.
games.why: prajna, the third quarter: no desire, no dream, knowing gathered into one, enjoying bliss.

practice: Let the body get heavy, as if drifting toward sleep, but stay just awake, wanting nothing from these minutes, letting images and thoughts pass without following them.
See if you can taste a little of what the text describes: no wanting, nothing to hold, just a quiet, gathered knowing. Don't try to fall asleep; just rest near it.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad. The third quarter is prajna: deep sleep, no desire, no dream, a single mass of knowing, made of bliss.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sushupta, deep sleep, fast asleep; Mandukya 5: the field of prajna.

carryVoice: Your line: ananda, the peace that wants nothing. Even dreamless sleep is full of it, the text says. Day two hundred fifty-six, done.
